pos: n. (the state of being before or with; rendering Hebrew panim, Greek prosopon)
etymology: From the Latin praesentia, from praesum, to be before. The Hebrew word is panim, face — to be in God's presence is to be before his face, and to be banished is to be sent out from it, which is why the Hebrew idiom for exile and for judgment is the same idiom.
biblical_def: Presence in Scripture is not the doctrine of omnipresence but the covenant nearness of God to his people, and the whole Bible can be read as the story of its loss and recovery. Because the Hebrew word is face, presence is personal and relational rather than spatial. The first exile is described in exactly these terms: “And Cain went out from the presence of the LORD, and dwelt in the land of Nod” (Genesis 4:16) — God is not absent from Nod, yet Cain has genuinely lost something. To Moses, hesitating at the prospect of leading a stiffnecked people, God gives the promise that settles everything: “My presence shall go with thee, and I will give thee rest” (Exodus 33:14). David, after his great sin, asks not to keep his throne but to keep the face of God: “Cast me not away from thy presence; and take not thy holy spirit from me” (Psalm 51:11). And the Psalter names what is finally there: “in thy presence is fulness of joy; at thy right hand there are pleasures for evermore” (Psalm 16:11). Hell in Scripture is destruction from the presence of the Lord; heaven is that presence unveiled. The tabernacle, the temple, the incarnation, the indwelling Spirit, and the new Jerusalem are the successive stages by which God brings his face back to men.
webster_summary: The state of being before God's face. Hebrew panim is literally face, so presence is covenant nearness rather than bare omnipresence — heaven is that face unveiled, hell is banishment from it.
webster_full: PRESENCE, n. prez'ens. [L. praesentia, from praesum, to be before.] The existence of a person or thing in a certain place; opposed to absence.
2. A being in company or in view; as, admitted to the presence of the king.
3. The person of a superior; approach face to face.
4. In theology, the presence of God, his special manifestation to his people, as distinguished from his omnipresence.
5. In Scripture, cast me not away from thy presence, Psa. 51; in thy presence is fulness of joy, Psa. 16.
corruption_summary: Presence has become a word for atmosphere — a mood produced in a room by music and lighting, spoken of as though it could be summoned. Scripture treats God's presence as a covenant gift, promised, withdrawn in judgment, and finally given in Christ.
corruption_paragraphs: Where a service is arranged to generate a felt sense of nearness and that sensation is then identified as the presence of God, two things go wrong at once. The regulative principle is set aside, since worship is now shaped by what produces the effect rather than by what God commanded; and the believer's assurance is tied to his feelings, so that a dry heart is read as a departed God. Exodus 33:14 gives the better ground: my presence shall go with thee is a promise, and promises are believed rather than felt.

The opposite error is nearer to the doctrinally careful. If presence is flattened into omnipresence — God is everywhere, therefore no more here than anywhere — then Genesis 4:16 and Psalm 51:11 become unintelligible, and so does the tabernacle. Scripture plainly means something by presence that it does not mean by omnipresence. The principle to recover is that God draws near covenantally to a particular people in a particular way, that this nearness was purchased at the cross by the One forsaken outside the camp, and that its final form is a city where his servants shall see his face.
roots_summary: Hebrew panim is face, and the idiom before the face of gives the whole vocabulary of presence and banishment. Greek prosopon is likewise face, and parousia is presence or arrival, the New Testament word for Christ's coming.
roots_lines: Hebrew panim (H6440) — face, presence; the plural form used of both God and men.
Hebrew lechem panim — bread of the face, rendered shewbread; loaves set continually before the LORD.
Hebrew shakan (H7931) — to dwell, to tabernacle; the root behind the later term shekinah.
Greek prosopon (G4383) — face, countenance, presence; used of seeing God face to face.
Greek parousia (G3952) — presence, arrival, coming; the standard term for the second advent.
usage: Of banishment as loss of the divine face: Cain went out from the presence of the LORD (Genesis 4:16).
Of the promise that settled Moses: my presence shall go with thee, and I will give thee rest (Exodus 33:14).
Of the final blessedness: in thy presence is fulness of joy (Psalm 16:11).
scriptures: Genesis 4:16
And Cain went out from the presence of the LORD, and dwelt in the land of Nod, on the east of Eden.
Exodus 33:14
And he said, My presence shall go with thee, and I will give thee rest.
Psalm 51:11
Cast me not away from thy presence; and take not thy holy spirit from me.
Psalm 16:11
Thou wilt shew me the path of life: in thy presence is fulness of joy; at thy right hand there are pleasures for evermore.

pos: n. (a holding, that which is owned; rendering Hebrew achuzzah, Greek peripoiesis)
etymology: From the Latin possessio, from possideo, to have and hold. Hebrew achuzzah is from achaz, to grasp or seize, and denotes a holding granted by another — in the Law, land held from the LORD, who declares that the land is his and Israel are strangers and sojourners with him.
biblical_def: Possession in Scripture is almost always a granted holding, not an absolute ownership, and the distinction runs through the whole covenant. To Abraham God says he will give the land of his sojourning “for an everlasting possession” (Genesis 17:8) — a gift with a giver, held on terms. Israel's tenure in Canaan is therefore conditional in its enjoyment though unbreakable in its promise, and the jubilee laws exist to keep any family from being permanently dispossessed, since the land could not finally be sold, only leased until the year of release. The Psalter extends the grant to the Son: “Ask of me, and I shall give thee the heathen for thine inheritance, and the uttermost parts of the earth for thy possession” (Psalm 2:8). Then the New Testament performs its characteristic reversal. Believers are not merely those who receive a possession; they are one. The Spirit is “the earnest of our inheritance until the redemption of the purchased possession” (Ephesians 1:14) — the church is God's own holding, bought with blood, and the Spirit is the down payment guaranteeing that the buyer will take delivery. Moses had said as much of Israel long before: “For the LORD'S portion is his people; Jacob is the lot of his inheritance” (Deuteronomy 32:9).
webster_summary: A holding granted by another. Israel's land was held from the LORD, never owned absolutely; and in the New Testament believers are themselves God's purchased possession, with the Spirit as the earnest.
webster_full: POSSESSION, n. [L. possessio.] The having, holding or detention of property in one's power or command; actual seizin or occupancy.
2. The thing possessed; land, estate, or goods owned; as, the possessions of a family.
3. The state of being under the dominion of another power; as, possession by an evil spirit.
4. In Scripture, an inheritance granted by God and held from him; as, an everlasting possession, Gen. 17.
5. Of the church, the purchased possession, redeemed unto God, Eph. 1.
corruption_summary: Ownership is now conceived as absolute — what is mine is mine to use, keep, or destroy. Scripture grants real property rights and grounds them in a prior divine ownership that makes every holding a stewardship.
corruption_paragraphs: Two errors flank this word and Scripture refuses both. The collectivist error denies private property outright, which the eighth commandment forbids: thou shalt not steal presupposes that something belonged to someone. The absolutist error says property is held without account, which the jubilee legislation flatly contradicts — the land could not be permanently alienated, because the LORD says the land is his. Between them stands stewardship: real ownership, really answerable.

The deeper recovery is the direction of the word in the New Testament. Ephesians 1:14 makes the believer the property rather than the proprietor, and 1 Corinthians states the ground: ye are not your own, for ye are bought with a price. That single fact reorders the questions men ask about their bodies, their time, their money, and their children. A man who understands himself as a purchased possession will still hold things, and hold them gladly, but he will hold them as a tenant whose Landlord is coming to take delivery.
roots_summary: Hebrew achuzzah is a holding, from achaz, to grasp; nachalah is the inheritance-portion allotted by lot. Greek peripoiesis is a possession or acquisition, and kleronomia the inheritance.
roots_lines: Hebrew achuzzah (H272) — a possession, a holding; the term for tribal land tenure in Canaan.
Hebrew achaz (H270) — to seize, to grasp, to hold fast; the verbal root.
Hebrew nachalah (H5159) — inheritance, heritage; the LORD's portion is his people.
Greek peripoiesis (G4047) — a purchased possession, an acquiring; used of the church in Ephesians 1:14.
Greek arrhabon (G728) — earnest, pledge, down payment; the Spirit as guarantee of the rest.
usage: Of the land granted to Abraham on terms: for an everlasting possession (Genesis 17:8).
Of the nations given to the Son: the uttermost parts of the earth for thy possession (Psalm 2:8).
Of the church as God's own holding: the redemption of the purchased possession (Ephesians 1:14).
scriptures: Genesis 17:8
And I will give unto thee, and to thy seed after thee, the land wherein thou art a stranger, all the land of Canaan, for an everlasting possession; and I will be their God.
Psalm 2:8
Ask of me, and I shall give thee the heathen for thine inheritance, and the uttermost parts of the earth for thy possession.
Ephesians 1:14
Which is the earnest of our inheritance until the redemption of the purchased possession, unto the praise of his glory.
Deuteronomy 32:9
For the LORD'S portion is his people; Jacob is the lot of his inheritance.

pos: n. (that which stands under; wealth, essence, reality; rendering Hebrew hon, Greek hupostasis)
etymology: From the Latin substantia, from sub and sto, to stand under. The Greek hupostasis is built the same way — hupo and histemi — and means that which stands underneath as a foundation, hence both reality and confident assurance.
biblical_def: Substance in the Authorized Version carries two senses that the same Latin root holds together. The commoner sense is material wealth: Job's “substance also was seven thousand sheep, and three thousand camels” (Job 1:3), and the prodigal “wasted his substance with riotous living” (Luke 15:13). Proverbs directs this substance godward: “Honour the LORD with thy substance, and with the firstfruits of all thine increase” (Proverbs 3:9) — the firstfruits, not the remainder, which is the whole logic of biblical giving. The second sense is philosophical and far weightier: that which stands under, the underlying reality. Hebrews uses it of faith in one of the most compressed sentences in Scripture: “Now faith is the substance of things hoped for, the evidence of things not seen” (Hebrews 11:1). Faith is not wishful sentiment about the future; it is the standing-under, the present title-deed, of what God has promised. The same Greek word is used of the Son as the express image of the Father's person, and the Nicene fathers took it up in the term homoousios, of one substance with the Father — the word on which the doctrine of the Trinity turned at Nicaea.
webster_summary: That which stands under — hence both a man's material estate and underlying reality itself. Faith is called the substance of things hoped for, and the Son is of one substance with the Father.
webster_full: SUBSTANCE, n. [L. substantia, of sub and sto, to stand under.] In a general sense, being; something existing by itself; that which underlies accidents.
2. That which constitutes anything what it is; essence; real or essential part.
3. Goods; estate; means; wealth; as, a man of substance.
4. Body; corporeal existence, as distinguished from a shadow.
5. In Scripture, faith is the substance of things hoped for, Heb. 11; honour the Lord with thy substance, Prov. 3.
corruption_summary: A materialist age keeps the wealth sense and loses the metaphysical one, so that substance means possessions and nothing stands under anything. Scripture uses the word for the unseen reality that upholds the seen.
corruption_paragraphs: When only the financial sense survives, Hebrews 11:1 becomes unreadable and gets softened into a statement about optimism — faith as a positive attitude toward an uncertain future. That is precisely what the verse denies. Faith is the hupostasis, the thing standing underneath, of what is hoped for, because the promise of God is more solid than the visible order; the chapter then lists men who staked their lives on it and died without receiving the promises, which no mere optimist does.

The loss also reaches the doctrine of God. Homoousios — of one substance with the Father — was the word Nicaea used to shut out Arianism, and it presupposes that substance means real being rather than stuff. An age that cannot think the category will not defend the creed, and will drift toward a Christ who is functionally divine without being of one substance, which is Arianism with better manners. The principle to recover is that the unseen is not the unreal; the world of goods rests on a reality that goods cannot measure, and the Son upholds all things by the word of his power.
roots_summary: Hebrew hon is wealth or sufficiency, and qinyan is acquired property. Greek hupostasis is that which stands under — substance, confidence, title-deed — and ousia is being or essence, the root of homoousios.
roots_lines: Hebrew hon (H1952) — wealth, substance, sufficiency; the word in Proverbs 3:9.
Hebrew qinyan (H7075) — property, acquisition; what a man has got.
Greek hupostasis (G5287) — that which stands under; substance, assurance, confidence.
Greek ousia (G3776) — being, essence, goods; the prodigal wasted his ousia.
Greek homoousios — of one substance; the Nicene term guarding the Son's full deity.
usage: Of material estate: his substance also was seven thousand sheep, and three thousand camels (Job 1:3).
Of firstfruits giving: honour the LORD with thy substance, and with the firstfruits of all thine increase (Proverbs 3:9).
Of faith as underlying reality: faith is the substance of things hoped for (Hebrews 11:1).
scriptures: Job 1:3

His substance also was seven thousand sheep, and three thousand camels, and five hundred yoke of oxen, and five hundred she asses, and a very great household; so that this man was the greatest of all the men of the east.
Proverbs 3:9
Honour the LORD with thy substance, and with the firstfruits of all thine increase:
Hebrews 11:1
Now faith is the substance of things hoped for, the evidence of things not seen.
Luke 15:13
And not many days after the younger son gathered all together, and took his journey into a far country, and there wasted his substance with riotous living.

pos: n. (a dwelling place; rendering Hebrew maon, Greek katoiketerion)
etymology: From the Latin habitatio, from habito, to dwell, a frequentative of habeo, to have — to dwell is to keep on having a place. Hebrew maon is a lair or dwelling, and zebul a lofty residence, the word Solomon used of the temple he had built.
biblical_def: Habitation is the settled dwelling place of a person, and Scripture uses it with striking symmetry: God has one, angels had one, and the church becomes one. Of God the word is used of heaven, from which he governs: “From the place of his habitation he looketh upon all the inhabitants of the earth” (Psalm 33:14), and Israel prays “Look down from thy holy habitation, from heaven, and bless thy people Israel” (Deuteronomy 26:15). Of the fallen angels it marks the enormity of their apostasy: they “kept not their first estate, but left their own habitation” (Jude 1:6) — creatures abandoning the station God assigned them, which is the essence of that sin and of every sin patterned after it. Then the astonishing turn: what God has in heaven he takes up among men, and not in a building. Paul tells the Ephesians that they are “builded together for an habitation of God through the Spirit” (Ephesians 2:22). The tabernacle in the wilderness and the temple on Zion were shadows of this; the substance is a people. The line runs from Eden through the wilderness tent and the stone temple to the incarnate Word who tabernacled among us, to the indwelt church, and ends in the city where God shall dwell with men and be their God.
webster_summary: A settled dwelling place. Scripture gives one to God in heaven, records that the fallen angels abandoned theirs, and then makes the church itself an habitation of God through the Spirit.
webster_full: HABITATION, n. [L. habitatio, from habito, to dwell.] Act of inhabiting; state of dwelling.
2. Place of abode; a settled dwelling; a mansion; a residence.
3. The abode of God; as, thy holy habitation, Deut. 26.
4. The station or estate assigned to a creature; as, the angels left their own habitation, Jude 6.
5. In Scripture, of the church, builded together for an habitation of God, Eph. 2.
corruption_summary: Church buildings are still commonly called God's house, and the New Testament reassigns the term to the people. The building is a convenience; the habitation is the congregation.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The pressure on this word comes from long habit inside the church rather than from outside it. When the sanctuary is spoken of as the house of God in a sense the New Testament reserves for the assembly, small distortions follow: reverence attaches to furniture, giving flows to masonry ahead of ministry, and a congregation scattered by fire or persecution feels it has lost God's dwelling when in fact the dwelling walked out of the doors.

The principle to recover is Ephesians 2:22 read alongside Jude 1:6. God's habitation is now a people built together, which raises the stakes of church membership and of division far above what most reckon; to split a congregation carelessly is to take a hammer to the place where God has chosen to live. And Jude's angels warn from the other side: a creature who leaves the station God appointed him falls, however exalted the station was. Both texts press the same point, that dwelling where God has put you is not a small part of godliness.
roots_summary: Hebrew maon is a dwelling or lair, zebul an exalted residence, and mishkan the tabernacle, from shakan, to dwell. Greek katoiketerion is a settled habitation and skenoo is to pitch a tent, John's verb for the incarnation.
roots_lines: Hebrew maon (H4583) — habitation, dwelling, den; used of God's heavenly abode.
Hebrew zebul (H2073) — a lofty residence; Solomon's word for the house he built.
Hebrew mishkan (H4908) — tabernacle, dwelling place; from shakan, to settle down.
Greek katoiketerion (G2732) — a settled habitation; the church in Ephesians 2:22.
Greek skenoo (G4637) — to pitch a tent, to tabernacle; the Word dwelt among us.
usage: Of heaven as God's dwelling: from the place of his habitation he looketh upon all the inhabitants of the earth (Psalm 33:14).
Of angels who abandoned their station: kept not their first estate, but left their own habitation (Jude 1:6).
Of the church as God's dwelling: builded together for an habitation of God through the Spirit (Ephesians 2:22).
scriptures: Psalm 33:14
From the place of his habitation he looketh upon all the inhabitants of the earth.
Deuteronomy 26:15
Look down from thy holy habitation, from heaven, and bless thy people Israel, and the land which thou hast given us, as thou swarest unto our fathers, a land that floweth with milk and honey.
Jude 1:6
And the angels which kept not their first estate, but left their own habitation, he hath reserved in everlasting chains under darkness unto the judgment of the great day.
Ephesians 2:22
In whom ye also are builded together for an habitation of God through the Spirit.

pos: n. (kind regard, goodwill; rendering Hebrew chen and ratson, Greek charis)
etymology: From the Latin favor, from faveo, to be kind toward. The Authorized Version keeps the older British spelling. Hebrew chen is grace or acceptance in another's eyes, and ratson is good pleasure or acceptance — the term used of a sacrifice God receives.
biblical_def: Favour is regard freely given, and in Scripture it moves in two directions. Godward, it is the Old Testament's ordinary word for grace: Noah found chen in the eyes of the LORD, and the noun rendered favour here is the same the New Testament renders grace. The Psalmist measures it against wrath and finds it decisive: “For his anger endureth but a moment; in his favour is life” (Psalm 30:5). Manward, favour is the good regard of one's neighbours, and Scripture treats it as a real good, worth seeking honestly: “So shalt thou find favour and good understanding in the sight of God and man” (Proverbs 3:4). Luke says the same of our Lord's boyhood — he “increased in wisdom and stature, and in favour with God and man” (Luke 2:52) — which shows that seeking to be well regarded is not in itself the sin of men-pleasing. But the word carries a warning in its other main use, where favour means charm or attractiveness: “Favour is deceitful, and beauty is vain: but a woman that feareth the LORD, she shall be praised” (Proverbs 31:30). The charm that wins regard is the very thing that may mislead, and the fear of the LORD is set against it as the durable ground of praise.
webster_summary: Kind regard freely given. Hebrew chen is the Old Testament word for grace; favour with men is a real good honestly sought, though the charm that wins it is called deceitful.
webster_full: FAVOR, FAVOUR, n. [L. favor, from faveo, to be kind to.] Kind regard; countenance; propitious aspect; friendly disposition.
2. Support; defense; vindication; as, to speak in favor of a friend.
3. A kind act or office; kindness done or granted; benevolence shown.
4. Object of kind regard; the person favored; also, grace or beauty of countenance.
5. In Scripture, the free grace of God; as, in his favor is life, Psa. 30; Noah found favor in the eyes of the Lord, Gen. 6.
corruption_summary: Favour now suggests partiality — the unfair leg-up, the connection that jumped the queue. Scripture's favour is unmerited by definition, which is not injustice but grace, since none had a claim in the first place.
corruption_paragraphs: The modern suspicion of favour comes from a real concern about corruption in human dealings, where showing favour usually means denying someone else their due. But the objection cannot be transferred to God without destroying the gospel, because no creature is owed anything, and where nothing is owed nothing is withheld. Divine favour is not God preferring some over others who had a claim; it is God giving to some what none could claim. Romans anticipates the complaint and answers it: is there unrighteousness with God? God forbid.

There is also a prosperity distortion running the other way, in which favour means smooth circumstances — the parking space, the promotion — so that trouble becomes evidence of lost favour. Psalm 30:5 says favour is life while anger is a moment, not that the favoured man never weeps; weeping may endure for a night. The principle to recover is that the favour Scripture chiefly means is the settled acceptance of a sinner in Christ, which does not fluctuate with the week's news.
roots_summary: Hebrew chen is grace or acceptance in another's eyes, from chanan, to stoop in kindness; ratson is good pleasure, the acceptance of a sacrifice. Greek charis covers both and becomes the New Testament word for grace.
roots_lines: Hebrew chen (H2580) — grace, favour, acceptance; what Noah found in the eyes of the LORD.
Hebrew ratson (H7522) — goodwill, acceptance, delight; used of an offering God receives.
Hebrew chesed (H2617) — covenant lovingkindness; favour bound by promise rather than by whim.
Greek charis (G5485) — grace, favour; the Septuagint's regular rendering of chen.
Greek eudokia (G2107) — good pleasure, goodwill; the angels' word over Bethlehem.
usage: Of divine favour set against momentary anger: his anger endureth but a moment; in his favour is life (Psalm 30:5).
Of the good regard of God and neighbour: Jesus increased in wisdom and stature, and in favour with God and man (Luke 2:52).
Of charm as an unreliable ground of praise: favour is deceitful, and beauty is vain (Proverbs 31:30).
scriptures: Psalm 30:5
For his anger endureth but a moment; in his favour is life: weeping may endure for a night, but joy cometh in the morning.
Proverbs 3:4
So shalt thou find favour and good understanding in the sight of God and man.
Luke 2:52
And Jesus increased in wisdom and stature, and in favour with God and man.
Proverbs 31:30
Favour is deceitful, and beauty is vain: but a woman that feareth the LORD, she shall be praised.

pos: n. (delight, good will, that which pleases; rendering Hebrew chephets and ratson, Greek eudokia and hedone)
etymology: From the French plaisir, from the Latin placeo, to please. Hebrew chephets means delight and also purpose — what one takes pleasure in is what one determines to do — and the Authorized Version's good pleasure preserves this fusion of delight and decree.
biblical_def: Pleasure in Scripture is first God's and only then man's, and the order matters. The creation exists for it: “for thy pleasure they are and were created” (Revelation 4:11). Election rests on it: God predestinated us unto the adoption of children “according to the good pleasure of his will” (Ephesians 1:5), which locates the cause of salvation in God's delight rather than in anything foreseen in the creature. Most searchingly, the atonement is traced to it: “Yet it pleased the LORD to bruise him; he hath put him to grief” (Isaiah 53:10) — not that the Father took delight in the Son's agony as agony, but that the redemption accomplished through it was his settled purpose and joy. Because the Hebrew word fuses delight and determination, God's pleasure is never a mood; it is his will, and it shall stand. Man's pleasure is treated more carefully. Scripture is not ascetic — God giveth us richly all things to enjoy — but it names the disordering of pleasure as a mark of the last days, when men shall be “lovers of pleasures more than lovers of God” (2 Timothy 3:4). The fault there is not that pleasure is loved but that it is loved more, and a good put in God's place becomes an idol.
webster_summary: Delight, and also settled good will. God's good pleasure fuses delight with decree — creation, election, and even the bruising of the Servant are traced to it; man's pleasure is good until loved above God.
webster_full: PLEASURE, n. plezh'ur. [Fr. plaisir; L. placeo, to please.] The gratification of the senses or of the mind; agreeable sensations or emotions; delight.
2. Approbation; as, it is the pleasure of the court.
3. Arbitrary will or choice; as, he may go or stay at his pleasure.
4. Sensual gratification; voluptuousness — often in a bad sense.
5. In Scripture, the good pleasure of God, his sovereign will and delight; as, according to the good pleasure of his will, Eph. 1.
corruption_summary: Modern life treats pleasure as the measure of a good life and Christianity as its enemy. Scripture makes pleasure a creature — genuinely good, God's own before it is ours, and ruinous only when it displaces him.
corruption_paragraphs: The world's error is to make pleasure ultimate, which destroys it; the pursuit of sensation apart from God yields the diminishing returns Ecclesiastes catalogued three thousand years ago. But the church has often answered with an asceticism Scripture does not teach, treating enjoyment itself as suspect and producing a piety that is grim rather than holy. Paul names the forbidding of meats and marriage as a doctrine of devils, and the same Psalm that speaks of God's presence promises pleasures for evermore at his right hand.

The doctrinal centre of the word is God's good pleasure, and this is where the sharpest correction falls on a man-centred gospel. Ephesians 1:5 grounds adoption in the good pleasure of God's will — not in foreseen faith, not in the sinner's decision, not in anything but God's delight in doing it. Isaiah 53:10 pushes further than most are comfortable going, saying it pleased the LORD to bruise him. The principle to recover is that God's pleasure is the deepest cause of everything, including the cross, and that a creature's pleasures are rightly ordered only when they run toward the God whose pleasure made them.
roots_summary: Hebrew chephets is delight and purpose together; ratson is good pleasure or acceptance. Greek eudokia is good pleasure or benevolent will, while hedone is pleasure in the sensual sense, giving English hedonism.
roots_lines: Hebrew chephets (H2656) — delight, desire, purpose; the pleasure of the LORD that shall prosper.
Hebrew ratson (H7522) — goodwill, favour, acceptable will; what is acceptable to God.
Greek eudokia (G2107) — good pleasure, benevolent purpose; the ground of election in Ephesians 1:5.
Greek thelema (G2307) — will; joined to eudokia in the phrase good pleasure of his will.
Greek hedone (G2237) — pleasure, sensual delight; the root of English hedonism.
usage: Of creation's final cause: for thy pleasure they are and were created (Revelation 4:11).
Of election grounded in God's delight: according to the good pleasure of his will (Ephesians 1:5).
Of pleasure disordered by being loved above God: lovers of pleasures more than lovers of God (2 Timothy 3:4).
scriptures: Revelation 4:11
Thou art worthy, O Lord, to receive glory and honour and power: for thou hast created all things, and for thy pleasure they are and were created.
Ephesians 1:5
Having predestinated us unto the adoption of children by Jesus Christ to himself, according to the good pleasure of his will,
Isaiah 53:10

Yet it pleased the LORD to bruise him; he hath put him to grief: when thou shalt make his soul an offering for sin, he shall see his seed, he shall prolong his days, and the pleasure of the LORD shall prosper in his hand.
2 Timothy 3:4
Traitors, heady, highminded, lovers of pleasures more than lovers of God;

pos: n. (firm trust, boldness of reliance; rendering Hebrew kesel and mibtach, Greek parrhesia and pepoithesis)
etymology: From the Latin confidentia, from con and fido, to trust — a trusting-with, a leaning upon. Hebrew mibtach is from batach, to lean or throw oneself upon, and Greek parrhesia is literally all-speech, the freedom of a man who may say everything because he stands accepted.
biblical_def: Confidence in Scripture is always identified by its object, and the whole moral weight of the word lies there. Placed in God it is commanded and commended: “For the LORD shall be thy confidence, and shall keep thy foot from being taken” (Proverbs 3:26). Placed in men it is folly, and the Psalmist ranks the two without qualification: “It is better to trust in the LORD than to put confidence in man” (Psalm 118:8). Paul applies the same test to religious credentials, which are the hardest confidence to surrender because they look like godliness — the circumcision are those who “worship God in the spirit, and rejoice in Christ Jesus, and have no confidence in the flesh” (Philippians 3:3) — and he then lists the pedigree he counted loss. The New Testament adds a second sense, boldness of access. Because the veil is rent, the believer may speak freely before God, and Hebrews urges him not to surrender that standing under pressure: “Cast not away therefore your confidence, which hath great recompence of reward” (Hebrews 10:35). Confidence in that sense is not self-assurance at all; it is the assurance of a man who knows whose blood brought him in.
webster_summary: Firm trust, and also boldness of access. Scripture judges confidence entirely by its object — the LORD, or man, or the flesh — and urges the believer not to cast away the boldness Christ purchased.
webster_full: CONFIDENCE, n. [L. confidentia, from confido; con and fido, to trust.] A trusting or reliance; an assurance of mind or firm belief in the integrity, stability or veracity of another.
2. Trust; reliance; applied to one's own powers or resources; self-reliance.
3. Boldness; courage to speak or act freely.
4. That in which trust is placed; ground of reliance; as, the Lord shall be thy confidence, Prov. 3.
5. In Scripture, no confidence in the flesh, Phil. 3; cast not away your confidence, Heb. 10.
corruption_summary: Confidence today means self-confidence — a quality to be built in oneself and projected. Scripture almost always treats confidence in oneself or in the flesh as the thing to be renounced, and locates true confidence outside the man.
corruption_paragraphs: Self-confidence is the modern virtue par excellence, taught to children as a foundation and to adults as a discipline. Scripture does not merely rank it lower; it names it as the rival. Philippians 3:3 defines the true circumcision partly by a negative — no confidence in the flesh — and the flesh Paul goes on to describe is not gross sin but an impeccable religious record. The most dangerous confidence a man can carry into the presence of God is the confidence that he has done rather well.

The correction is not that Christians should be diffident. Hebrews 10:35 commands the retention of confidence, and the same chapter has just described believers entering the holiest by the blood of Jesus. The principle to recover is the difference in ground. Self-confidence rests on an assessment of oneself and must therefore be maintained by favourable evidence; Christian confidence rests on the finished work of another and can survive an honest look in the mirror. That is why it can grow as self-knowledge deepens, where the other cannot.
roots_summary: Hebrew batach is to lean or throw oneself upon, giving mibtach, the object of trust; kesel is confidence and, in a bad sense, folly. Greek parrhesia is freedom of speech before God, and pepoithesis is settled reliance.
roots_lines: Hebrew batach (H982) — to trust, to lean upon, to feel safe; the root of the trust vocabulary.
Hebrew mibtach (H4009) — that in which one trusts; the object, not the feeling.
Hebrew kesel (H3689) — confidence; the same form can mean folly, a warning built into the word.
Greek parrhesia (G3954) — freedom of speech, boldness of access; from pas and rhesis, all-speech.
Greek pepoithesis (G4006) — confidence, settled reliance; from the perfect of peitho, to persuade.
usage: Of God as the object of trust: the LORD shall be thy confidence, and shall keep thy foot from being taken (Proverbs 3:26).
Of religious credentials renounced: have no confidence in the flesh (Philippians 3:3).
Of boldness of access not to be surrendered: cast not away therefore your confidence (Hebrews 10:35).
scriptures: Proverbs 3:26
For the LORD shall be thy confidence, and shall keep thy foot from being taken.
Psalm 118:8
It is better to trust in the LORD than to put confidence in man.
Philippians 3:3
For we are the circumcision, which worship God in the spirit, and rejoice in Christ Jesus, and have no confidence in the flesh.
Hebrews 10:35
Cast not away therefore your confidence, which hath great recompence of reward.

pos: n. (settled intention, design; rendering Hebrew etsah and chephets, Greek prothesis)
etymology: From the Old French porpos, from the Latin propono, to set before — a purpose is something set out in front and moved toward. Greek prothesis is built identically, pro and tithemi, a setting-before; it is also the word for the shewbread set before the LORD.
biblical_def: Purpose is settled intention, and Scripture uses it chiefly of God, whose purpose is the hidden spine of history. Paul's great consolation rests entirely on it: “And we know that all things work together for good to them that love God, to them who are the called according to his purpose” (Romans 8:28) — the working-together of all things is not a general optimism about the universe but a consequence of a purpose that governs it, and the promise is bounded by the calling. He states the scope of that purpose plainly: believers are “predestinated according to the purpose of him who worketh all things after the counsel of his own will” (Ephesians 1:11). All things, not most things, and after the counsel of his own will, not in response to ours. Ecclesiastes sets the same truth in time: “To every thing there is a season, and a time to every purpose under the heaven” (Ecclesiastes 3:1). Man's purpose is a smaller word but a real one, and Scripture commends it as resolve: Barnabas “exhorted them all, that with purpose of heart they would cleave unto the Lord” (Acts 11:23). Divine purpose does not abolish human resolve; it is precisely what makes resolve worth having.
webster_summary: Settled intention. God's purpose governs all things after the counsel of his own will and is the ground of Romans 8:28; man's purpose is real resolve, commended as cleaving to the Lord with purpose of heart.
webster_full: PURPOSE, n. [Fr. propos; L. propono, to set before.] That which a person sets before himself as an object to be reached or accomplished; design; intention.
2. Intention; aim; end proposed; as, to what purpose is this waste?
3. Effect; consequence, good or bad; as, to little purpose.
4. Instance; example — an older use.
5. In Scripture, the eternal counsel of God; as, called according to his purpose, Rom. 8.
corruption_summary: Purpose has become a therapeutic project — the individual's search for personal meaning, discovered by looking inward. Scripture's purpose is God's, fixed before the foundation of the world, and the creature's peace lies in being caught up into it.
corruption_paragraphs: The self-actualising sense of purpose puts an unbearable weight on the individual, who must now generate significance out of his own preferences, and it fails exactly where it is most needed — in suffering, in obscurity, in old age, in a life that looks small. Romans 8:28 offers the opposite structure. The believer is not told to find his purpose; he is told he is called according to God's, and that this is why the wreckage works together for good. The comfort is external, and therefore available to a man who has run out of inner resources.

There is also a sub-Christian version that grants God a purpose but makes it responsive — God adjusting his plan to human decisions, which is the position open theism argues explicitly and which much popular preaching assumes without argument. Ephesians 1:11 shuts the door: he worketh all things after the counsel of his own will. The principle to recover is that a purpose which could be defeated could not comfort anyone. Precisely because God's purpose is unconditional, Barnabas's exhortation makes sense — cleave to the Lord with purpose of heart, since the One you cleave to will not be turned aside.
roots_summary: Hebrew etsah is counsel or plan and chephets is purpose fused with delight. Greek prothesis is a setting-before, used both of God's eternal purpose and of the shewbread; boule is deliberate counsel.
roots_lines: Hebrew etsah (H6098) — counsel, purpose, plan; the counsel of the LORD standeth for ever.
Hebrew chephets (H2656) — delight and purpose together; the pleasure of the LORD that shall prosper.
Greek prothesis (G4286) — a setting-before; God's eternal purpose, and the shewbread set before him.
Greek boule (G1012) — deliberate counsel, determinate will; joined to foreknowledge in Acts 2:23.
Greek proorizo (G4309) — to mark out beforehand, to predestinate; the verb tied to purpose in Ephesians 1:11.
usage: Of the ground on which all things work together for good: the called according to his purpose (Romans 8:28).
Of the scope of that purpose: him who worketh all things after the counsel of his own will (Ephesians 1:11).
Of human resolve commended: with purpose of heart they would cleave unto the Lord (Acts 11:23).
scriptures: Romans 8:28
And we know that all things work together for good to them that love God, to them who are the called according to his purpose.
Ephesians 1:11
In whom also we have obtained an inheritance, being predestinated according to the purpose of him who worketh all things after the counsel of his own will:
Ecclesiastes 3:1
To every thing there is a season, and a time to every purpose under the heaven:
Acts 11:23
Who, when he came, and had seen the grace of God, was glad, and exhorted them all, that with purpose of heart they would cleave unto the Lord.

pos: n. and v. (a ground or cause; the faculty of thought; to argue; rendering Hebrew yakach, Greek logos and dialegomai)
etymology: From the Latin ratio, a reckoning, through the French raison. The Hebrew verb in Isaiah 1:18, yakach, belongs to the law court — to argue a case, to reprove, to set matters right between parties — so the divine invitation to reason together is a summons to litigation that ends in pardon.
biblical_def: Reason appears in the Authorized Version as a ground or cause, as the faculty of thinking, and as a verb meaning to argue a case. Scripture never treats human reason as autonomous, and never treats it as worthless either. God addresses it directly: “Come now, and let us reason together, saith the LORD: though your sins be as scarlet, they shall be as white as snow” (Isaiah 1:18). The invitation is judicial — God summons his people to argue the matter out — and it ends not in a negotiated settlement but in cleansing offered by the offended party. Peter requires reasoned defence of every Christian, not only of teachers: “be ready always to give an answer to every man that asketh you a reason of the hope that is in you” (1 Peter 3:15), and the preceding clause governs it, sanctify the Lord God in your hearts — apologetics begins in submission, not in neutrality. The apostles also use the word for sound practical judgment in church order: “It is not reason that we should leave the word of God, and serve tables” (Acts 6:2), the sentence that produced the diaconate. Reason so used is a servant of Scripture, ordering the church's life under a rule it did not invent.
webster_summary: A ground or cause, the faculty of thought, and to argue a case. Scripture summons men to reason and requires a reasoned defence of hope — reason as servant of revelation, never as its judge.
webster_full: REASON, n. [Fr. raison; L. ratio, from reor, to think or judge.] A ground or cause; that which supports or justifies an act or opinion.
2. The faculty of the mind by which it distinguishes truth from falsehood, and good from evil.
3. Right; justice; equity; as, it is not reason that we should leave the word of God, Acts 6.
4. To reason, v.i. To argue; to debate; to deduce consequences from premises.
5. In Scripture, come now, and let us reason together, Isa. 1; a reason of the hope that is in you, 1 Pet. 3.
corruption_summary: The Enlightenment made reason the judge of revelation; a reaction now treats reason as merely one perspective among many. Scripture makes it a real faculty, damaged by the fall, and a servant under the word of God.
corruption_paragraphs: The rationalist error seats reason above Scripture and asks the Bible to justify itself at that bar, which produced the whole apparatus of historical criticism — miracles filtered out because reason had ruled beforehand that miracles do not occur. The Reformed answer is not that reason is bad but that it is a creature and a fallen one; the noetic effects of sin mean the instrument is bent, and a bent rule cannot measure the straight edge that must correct it.

The opposite error, now more fashionable, dissolves reason into perspective and treats every argument as a bid for power, so that giving reasons is thought naive. That position cannot be stated without using the reason it denies, and it leaves 1 Peter 3:15 impossible, since a reason of the hope must be given to every man that asketh. The principle to recover is the order Peter sets: sanctify the Lord God in your hearts first, and reason from that submission. Isaiah 1:18 shows God himself doing what neither error expects — arguing with sinners, and offering to make scarlet white.
roots_summary: Hebrew yakach is to argue, decide, or reprove, a courtroom verb. Greek logos is word, account, or reason — the reason a man renders — and dialegomai is to reason or dispute, Paul's regular activity in the synagogues.
roots_lines: Hebrew yakach (H3198) — to argue a case, to reprove, to set right; the verb of Isaiah 1:18.
Hebrew taam (H2940) — taste, discernment, judgment; sound sense as a faculty.
Greek logos (G3056) — word, account, reason; the reason rendered in 1 Peter 3:15.
Greek dialegomai (G1256) — to reason, to discuss, to dispute; used of Paul in the synagogue at Thessalonica.
Greek apologia (G627) — a defence, a reasoned answer; the root of English apologetics.
usage: Of God summoning sinners to argue the case: come now, and let us reason together, saith the LORD (Isaiah 1:18).
Of the defence required of every believer: a reason of the hope that is in you (1 Peter 3:15).
Of sound judgment in church order: it is not reason that we should leave the word of God (Acts 6:2).
scriptures: Isaiah 1:18
Come now, and let us reason together, saith the LORD: though your sins be as scarlet, they shall be as white as snow; though they be red like crimson, they shall be as wool.
1 Peter 3:15
But sanctify the Lord God in your hearts: and be ready always to give an answer to every man that asketh you a reason of the hope that is in you with meekness and fear:
Acts 6:2
Then the twelve called the multitude of the disciples unto them, and said, It is not reason that we should leave the word of God, and serve tables.
Proverbs 3:4
So shalt thou find favour and good understanding in the sight of God and man.

pos: n. and v. (regular arrangement, rank, succession; to arrange; rendering Hebrew arak and dibrah, Greek taxis)
etymology: From the Latin ordo, a row or rank, a term first of weaving and then of the army. Hebrew arak is to arrange or set in rows — used of laying wood on the altar and of drawing up a battle line — and Greek taxis is a military rank or fixed arrangement.
biblical_def: Order is regular arrangement, and Scripture presents it as a reflection of God's own character rather than a matter of taste. Paul grounds it there explicitly: God is not the author of confusion, and therefore “Let all things be done decently and in order” (1 Corinthians 14:40) — the closing rule of a chapter governing the conduct of public worship, which is why the regulative principle is a matter of obedience and not preference. Order in the church is also structural. Titus was left in Crete “that thou shouldest set in order the things that are wanting, and ordain elders in every city” (Titus 1:5), so that a congregation without properly ordained elders is, in the apostle's judgment, still lacking something. Paul commends the Colossians for it as a spiritual grace, “joying and beholding your order, and the stedfastness of your faith in Christ” (Colossians 2:5), setting order beside steadfastness as things a pastor rejoices to see. The word also names a priestly succession: Christ is “a priest for ever after the order of Melchizedek” (Psalm 110:4), a priesthood not by Levitical descent but by divine oath, and Hebrews builds its central argument on that phrase.
webster_summary: Regular arrangement, rank, and succession. Because God is not the author of confusion, order in worship and in church government is obedience; and Christ is a priest after the order of Melchizedek.
webster_full: ORDER, n. [L. ordo.] Regular disposition or methodical arrangement of things; a word of extensive application.
2. Proper state; as, the house is in order.
3. Rank; class; degree; also, a rule or regulation; a command.
4. Regular government or discipline; as, order in the church.
5. In Scripture, let all things be done decently and in order, 1 Cor. 14; a priest after the order of Melchizedek, Psa. 110.
corruption_summary: Order is heard as constraint — the enemy of authenticity and of the Spirit's freedom. Scripture derives order from the character of God himself and makes it the condition, not the rival, of true liberty.
corruption_paragraphs: The spontaneity objection appears wherever structured worship is thought to quench the Spirit, and 1 Corinthians 14 is the decisive answer, because it is the chapter most concerned with the extraordinary gifts and it ends by commanding order. Paul's reason is theological rather than practical: God is not the author of confusion but of peace, so disorder in worship misrepresents God. A congregation that prizes unpredictability above the commanded elements has not become more spiritual; it has become less like the God it gathers to worship.

A second pressure is on church government. Titus 1:5 treats the ordination of elders as part of setting in order what is wanting, which is not compatible with treating polity as adiaphora to be arranged by preference or efficiency. The New Testament pattern is a plurality of elders and deacons in each local congregation. The principle to recover is that order is not the opposite of life — it is the shape life takes when it comes from a God of peace, and Paul rejoiced to behold it as gladly as he rejoiced to behold faith.
roots_summary: Hebrew arak is to arrange in rows, used of altar wood and of battle lines; dibrah is manner or order, the term in Psalm 110:4. Greek taxis is fixed arrangement or rank, and euschemonos means decently, becomingly.
roots_lines: Hebrew arak (H6186) — to set in order, to arrange in rows; used of the wood upon the altar.
Hebrew dibrah (H1700) — manner, order, cause; after the order of Melchizedek.
Hebrew maarakah (H4634) — a row, an army in battle array; order as a martial figure.
Greek taxis (G5010) — fixed arrangement, rank, order; used of both church order and Melchizedek's priesthood.
Greek euschemonos (G2156) — decently, in a becoming manner; joined to taxis in 1 Corinthians 14:40.
usage: Of the rule closing the chapter on public worship: let all things be done decently and in order (1 Corinthians 14:40).
Of church government still wanting until elders are ordained: set in order the things that are wanting (Titus 1:5).
Of Christ's priestly succession: a priest for ever after the order of Melchizedek (Psalm 110:4).
scriptures: 1 Corinthians 14:40
Let all things be done decently and in order.
Titus 1:5
For this cause left I thee in Crete, that thou shouldest set in order the things that are wanting, and ordain elders in every city, as I had appointed thee:
Colossians 2:5
For though I be absent in the flesh, yet am I with you in the spirit, joying and beholding your order, and the stedfastness of your faith in Christ.
Psalm 110:4
The LORD hath sworn, and will not repent, Thou art a priest for ever after the order of Melchizedek.
